title: The Abhidhamma's seven books
hookLine: a walk along the seven books of the Abhidhamma, ending in the great book of conditions
carry: seven books, ending in the web of conditions

cards: Before anyone reads a book, there's the spine on the shelf. A title, nothing more, and already it tells you something. The third basket is made of seven books, and their titles read like a strange little poem.
A list. An analysis. A talk about elements.
A book of persons. A book of arguments. A book of pairs.
And the great book of conditions. Today, no deep dive: just a slow walk along the shelf, pulling each book out far enough to see how it begins.

teach.b: First, the Dhammasangani, the enumeration of things. It opens with the list of mental states, wholesome, unwholesome and neither, then takes a single wholesome moment and names everything present in it.

Second, the Vibhanga, the book of analysis. It takes familiar teachings, the aggregates, the senses, the noble truths, and analyzes each one, often first in the style of the suttas and then in the Abhidhamma's own.
Third, the Dhatukatha, the discussion of elements: how each thing fits, or doesn't, into the larger groupings. Fourth, a surprise: the Puggalapannatti, the designation of persons.

In a basket that takes people apart into moments, here's a whole book sorting kinds of people: the one who keeps a promise, the one who doesn't. In two days, this path will show why that's no contradiction.
Fifth, the Kathavatthu, the points of controversy, where the views of other early Buddhist schools are set out and answered, one argument at a time.
Tradition says it was put together at a council long after the Buddha, by an elder named Moggaliputta Tissa, following an outline the Buddha had laid down.

teach.h: A BOOK OF ARGUMENTS AND PAIRS.
teach.b: Sixth, the Yamaka, the book of pairs. It asks its questions forward and backward: is every this a that, and is every that a this? A book about using words exactly.
And seventh, the Patthana, the book of conditions, which tradition calls the great book. It asks how each thing helps another arise: by being its root, by coming just before it, by supporting it.
Tradition says that when the Buddha turned his mind to it, colored light streamed from his body.

how: Theravada monks and nuns study the seven books of the Abhidhamma, and in some Theravada communities passages from them, including the opening list of the Dhammasangani, are chanted at ceremonies.

o: the first sermons the Buddha gave after awakening
the books that make up the Pali canon's third basket
the monastic rules, gathered in a set of volumes

p: opens with the list of mental states
a book sorting kinds of persons

s: the seven books are collections of stories about the Buddha
they're lists, analyses, arguments and questions: from the list of mental states to the book of conditions.
one of the seven books argues with the views of other early schools
the Kathavatthu, the points of controversy.
the Yamaka asks its questions only one way
it's the book of pairs: every question asked forward and backward.

games.q: you're putting together a basket of books that takes people apart into moments of mind. a book that sorts kinds of people is on the table. what do you do with it?
o: leave it out: it doesn't fit
rewrite it so it never mentions persons
games.why: it's in: the Puggalapannatti, the designation of persons, sits fourth among the seven books. in two days, this path shows how talk of persons and talk of moments can sit side by side.

practice: If you'd like, say the seven titles inwardly, one for each slow breath, in English or in Pali: the enumeration of things, analysis, elements, persons, points of controversy, pairs, conditions.
Then rest on the last one, and notice one thing in this moment that something else helped bring about: the warmth of the chair, the light from the window, this breath.

wordCard.voice: Seven books. The third basket of the Pali canon, from the list of mental states to the great book of conditions. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the seventh book, usually given in English as conditions, or conditional relations.

carryVoice: Your line: seven books, ending in the web of conditions. A list of mental states at the start; at the end, each moment leaning on others. See you tomorrow.
